payload.prompt: Complete the definition.

parts.text: The capability that converts spoken words into written text is

payload.explanation: The input is spoken audio and the output is written text, so the capability is recognition, also called speech-to-text.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The conversion direction is not right for spoken words becoming text.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Do not use synthesis here because synthesis starts with written text. Audio capture only records sound; recognition transcribes it.

payload.prompt: Complete the definition.

parts.text: The capability that converts written text into spoken audio is

payload.explanation: The input is written text and the output is spoken audio, so the capability is synthesis, also called text-to-speech.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The answer reverses or narrows the text-to-audio process.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Recognition turns speech into text, and text normalization only prepares text for pronunciation. The full capability for spoken output is synthesis.

payload.prompt: Type the term that completes this sentence.

parts.text: AI applications that use recognition, synthesis, or both for voice interaction are

payload.explanation: The phrase names the whole application or agent that supports voice interaction, not just one listening or speaking capability.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The answer names only part of the voice experience instead of the full solution.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Recognition and synthesis are capabilities. The broader term for an application using them for voice interaction is speech-enabled solution.

payload.prompt: Which term completes this sentence?

parts.text: Even when speech is available, apps should provide
for users who prefer or require them.

payload.explanation: Speech can help accessibility, but some users still need or prefer text-based ways to give input and receive output.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Some users would be left without the input or output method they need.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Avoid a speech-only answer here. The key idea is that speech should be paired with text alternatives.

payload.prompt: Put the pieces in the correct order.
payload.explanation: The sentence identifies the role speech recognition plays in a voice application: it handles the listening side.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The sentence no longer clearly names recognition as the app's listening side.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with the capability, then connect it to its role in the voice app.

payload.prompt: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.
payload.explanation: The order shows the output role of synthesis: it is the speaking side of a voice-enabled app.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The sentence no longer clearly names synthesis as the app's speaking side.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Put the capability first, then name its role in spoken output.

payload.prompt: Order the pieces correctly.
payload.explanation: The sentence names speech capabilities first, then connects them to benefits such as hands-free operation and productivity.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The benefit statement becomes unclear or incomplete.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Begin with speech capabilities, then show what they can enable for users.

payload.prompt: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.
payload.explanation: The sentence uses a contrast: speech supports accessibility, but it should not remove text-based alternatives.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The contrast between speech support and text alternatives becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Keep both ideas in order: speech can help, and text alternatives are still needed.

payload.prompt: Which statements describe speech recognition?

options.rationale: Speech-to-text is another name for speech recognition. The name points to the direction: speech becomes text.

options.text: It transcribes audio into written text
options.rationale: Transcription means converting spoken audio into written text. This is the main role of speech recognition.

options.text: It creates natural-sounding audio from text
options.error_type: confuses recognition with synthesis
options.rationale: Creating natural-sounding audio from text is speech synthesis. Recognition works in the opposite direction.
options.better_fit: Use this statement to describe speech synthesis, also called text-to-speech.

feedback.intrinsic: The listening capability would be mixed up with the speaking capability.
feedback.instructional: Use the direction to tell them apart: recognition is speech-to-text, and synthesis is text-to-speech.

options.text: It is the listening side of a voice app
options.rationale: Recognition handles spoken input from users. That is why it is the listening side of a voice-enabled application.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech recognition is speech-to-text: it listens to spoken input and transcribes it into written text.

payload.prompt: Which statements describe speech synthesis output?

options.rationale: Speech synthesis turns written text into audio users can hear. Spoken responses, alerts, and directions are common examples of this output.

options.text: It can create a natural-sounding audio waveform
options.rationale: A synthesis system can generate speech that sounds natural rather than robotic. The final product is an audio waveform that represents spoken language.

options.text: It creates a written transcript from a phone call
options.error_type: confuses synthesis with recognition
options.rationale: A written transcript from call audio is created by speech recognition. Synthesis works from written text toward spoken audio.
options.better_fit: Use this statement for speech recognition in call centers, meetings, or dictation tools.

feedback.intrinsic: The output would be text from audio, not audio from text.
feedback.instructional: Use the output to tell the capabilities apart. Synthesis produces spoken audio; recognition produces written text.

options.text: It is the speaking side of a voice app
options.rationale: Synthesis handles spoken output. It lets an application communicate information audibly to users.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech synthesis produces spoken audio or a natural-sounding waveform and serves as the speaking side of a voice app.

payload.prompt: Which user needs can speech features help support?

options.rationale: Speech output can read content aloud for users with visual impairments. This can make text-heavy content easier to consume audibly.
Speech input can reduce the need for keyboards and screens. That can help users with mobility challenges.
Audio alternatives can support users with reading disabilities like dyslexia. Speech synthesis can read written content aloud.

options.text: A requirement to use only screens
options.error_type: confuses accessibility support with screen-only interaction
options.rationale: Speech features reduce reliance on screens in many scenarios. Accessibility also means providing alternatives, not requiring only screens.
options.better_fit: Use screens or text as optional alternatives for users who prefer or require them.

feedback.intrinsic: The design would narrow access instead of giving users more usable ways to interact.
feedback.instructional: Accessibility is about supporting different needs. Speech can help, and text or screen options should remain available.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech can support visual, mobility, and reading needs, while text alternatives should still remain available.

payload.prompt: Which statements explain how speech can help global audiences?

options.rationale: Multiple language support helps speech features reach more users. This is one way speech capabilities can serve global audiences.
Regional dialect support helps speech features work better for more speakers. Dialects are part of reaching global audiences.

options.error_type: confuses benefits with privacy and compliance considerations
options.rationale: Privacy and compliance still matter when audio data is processed, stored, and protected. Speech benefits do not remove those responsibilities.
options.better_fit: Use this as an implementation consideration before adding speech features.

feedback.intrinsic: The team might overlook how audio data is processed, stored, or protected.
feedback.instructional: Global reach is a benefit of language and dialect support. Privacy remains a separate consideration.

options.text: It can make voice interaction more usable for more people
options.rationale: Supporting languages and regional dialects can make voice interaction more usable. That helps speech features reach a wider audience.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Multiple language and regional dialect support can make voice interaction useful for more people.

payload.prompt: True or false?
payload.statement: Speech synthesis by itself can understand a user's spoken request and decide what it means.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech synthesis produces spoken output; understanding spoken requests requires other capabilities such as speech recognition and language understanding.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The speaking capability was treated as if it could also handle understanding spoken input.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Speech synthesis is the output side of a voice app. It can speak text aloud, but it does not by itself interpret a user's spoken request.

payload.prompt: Decide whether this statement is true or false.
payload.statement: Speech recognition is also called speech-to-text.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech recognition is also called speech-to-text because it converts spoken words into written text.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A correct alternate name for recognition was marked false.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Speech-to-text is the common name for recognition because it transcribes audio into written text.

payload.prompt: Is the following statement accurate?
payload.statement: Speech capabilities only improve visual screen layout and do not support hands-free operation.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech capabilities can support hands-free operation, accessibility, productivity, natural interaction, and global audiences; they are not limited to visual screen layout.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The answer treats speech capabilities as if they were mainly about screens.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Speech benefits focus on voice interaction, such as hands-free use and reduced reliance on keyboards or screens.

payload.prompt: Evaluate this statement.
payload.statement: Accessibility includes needs such as visual impairments, mobility challenges, hearing loss, and reading disabilities.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Accessibility means designing for varied needs, including visual, mobility, hearing, and reading-related needs.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Several accessibility needs were left out of the design view.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Speech can help some needs, but accessibility starts by recognizing the range of users who may need different interaction methods.

payload.prompt: True or false?
payload.statement: A speech-enabled solution must use speech synthesis only, without speech recognition.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. A speech-enabled solution can use recognition, synthesis, or both for voice interaction.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The meaning of speech-enabled solution was narrowed too much.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Speech-enabled solutions are broader than spoken output. They may listen, speak, or do both.

payload.prompt: Decide whether this statement is true or false.
payload.statement: Speech synthesis can create natural-sounding audio from written text.
payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech synthesis, or text-to-speech, converts written text into natural-sounding spoken audio.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A core definition of synthesis was marked false.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: When written text becomes spoken audio, the capability is speech synthesis.

payload.prompt: A customer service manager wants callers to speak their questions and hear helpful answers from an AI agent. What is the team building?

options.rationale: This is the broad name for an application or agent that supports voice interaction. Callers speak, and the agent answers aloud, so the design can combine recognition and synthesis.

options.error_type: confuses full speech-enabled solution with listening only
options.rationale: Speech recognition converts caller speech into text. It does not cover the spoken answers callers hear.
options.better_fit: Use this when the feature only needs to transcribe what a caller says into written text.

feedback.intrinsic: Callers could speak their questions, but they would not hear the helpful spoken answer the manager wants.
feedback.instructional: Recognition is the listening part. A full voice interaction also needs the speaking part when callers must hear answers.

options.error_type: confuses full speech-enabled solution with speaking only
options.rationale: Speech synthesis converts written text into spoken audio. It does not capture what callers say first.
options.better_fit: Use this when the feature only needs to read written answers or alerts aloud.

feedback.intrinsic: The agent could speak, but it would miss the caller's spoken question.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis is the speaking part. When users speak into the experience, recognition is also involved.

options.error_type: confuses user interaction with microphone signal capture
options.rationale: Audio capture is the first step of recognition, where sound is captured as a digital signal. It is not the whole voice interaction.
options.better_fit: Use this when focusing only on capturing sound through a microphone before recognition.

feedback.intrinsic: The call audio might be captured, but it would not become a complete conversation with useful answers.
feedback.instructional: Capturing sound is only an early step. Speech-enabled solutions are about using speech capabilities for voice interaction.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The callers speak and hear spoken answers, so this is a speech-enabled solution using voice interaction.

payload.prompt: A support center needs live written records while customers speak on calls. Which capability should it use?

options.error_type: confuses speech-to-text with text-to-speech
options.rationale: Speech synthesis turns written text into spoken audio. The support center needs the opposite direction: spoken calls becoming written records.
options.better_fit: Use this when a support bot needs to read an answer aloud to a customer.

feedback.intrinsic: The center would get spoken output, but not the live written call records it needs.
feedback.instructional: Match the direction of the conversion. Speech-to-text is recognition; text-to-speech is synthesis.

options.rationale: Speech recognition is also called speech-to-text. It listens to audio input and transcribes spoken words into written text.

options.error_type: confuses transcription with preparing text for pronunciation
options.rationale: Text normalization prepares written text for speech by expanding abbreviations, numbers, and symbols. It belongs to the synthesis pipeline, not live call transcription.
options.better_fit: Use this before speech synthesis pronounces items like dates, prices, or abbreviations.

feedback.intrinsic: Customer speech would not become usable written records during the call.
feedback.instructional: Normalization starts with text that already exists. Recognition is needed when the input is spoken audio.

options.error_type: confuses transcription with audio waveform generation
options.rationale: A neural vocoder generates the final audio waveform in speech synthesis. It does not transcribe customer speech into text.
options.better_fit: Use this when generating natural-sounding spoken audio from linguistic representations.

feedback.intrinsic: The center would focus on producing audio instead of creating the call transcript.
feedback.instructional: Vocoding is part of spoken output. Transcription of calls requires speech recognition.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech recognition turns spoken calls into written text, which supports live records and searchable call notes.

payload.prompt: A navigation app must announce directions so drivers do not need to look at the screen. Which capability should it use?

options.error_type: confuses text-to-speech with speech-to-text
options.rationale: Speech recognition listens to spoken input and turns it into written text. The navigation app needs to speak directions aloud.
options.better_fit: Use this when drivers speak commands to the app, such as asking for a route.

feedback.intrinsic: Drivers could give voice commands, but they still would not hear the directions announced.
feedback.instructional: Recognition handles spoken input. Announcing directions is spoken output, so it needs synthesis.

options.error_type: confuses generating speech with recording sound
options.rationale: Audio capture records sound from a microphone as a digital signal. It does not generate spoken directions from written route information.
options.better_fit: Use this at the start of a recognition pipeline when the app needs to listen.

feedback.intrinsic: The app might capture sound, but drivers would still need another way to receive directions.
feedback.instructional: Capturing audio is not the same as producing audio. Spoken directions require text-to-speech.

options.rationale: Speech synthesis is also called text-to-speech. It converts written text, such as directions or alerts, into spoken audio.

options.error_type: confuses spoken output with predicting word sequences
options.rationale: Language modeling helps choose likely word sequences during speech recognition. It is not the capability that reads directions aloud.
options.better_fit: Use this when improving transcription by applying vocabulary, grammar, and common word patterns.

feedback.intrinsic: The app might better predict words during transcription, but it would not announce route instructions.
feedback.instructional: Language modeling supports recognition. For audible directions, use synthesis.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech synthesis converts written directions into spoken audio, so drivers can listen without looking at the screen.

payload.prompt: A warehouse worker updates orders while carrying boxes and cannot use a keyboard. Which speech benefit fits best?

options.rationale: Speech can remove the need for keyboards and screens in some workflows. That directly fits a worker whose hands are busy carrying boxes.

options.error_type: confuses a benefit with an implementation factor
options.rationale: Microphone quality affects recognition accuracy. It is a factor to evaluate before implementation, not the main user benefit here.
options.better_fit: Consider this when planning audio quality requirements for speech recognition.

feedback.intrinsic: The worker's main problem, busy hands, would not be described clearly by this choice.
feedback.instructional: Microphone quality affects how well recognition works. The benefit in this scenario is hands-free operation.

options.error_type: confuses a speech benefit with recognition cleanup
options.rationale: Profanity filtering is a post-processing task that can mask or remove inappropriate words. It does not describe why speech helps someone who cannot type.
options.better_fit: Use this when transcribed text must be cleaned up according to a policy.

feedback.intrinsic: The order update workflow would still be framed around text cleanup, not the worker's need to work while carrying boxes.
feedback.instructional: Post-processing improves transcript output. The workplace benefit here is using speech without a keyboard.

options.error_type: confuses user benefit with a decoding technique
options.rationale: Beam search is a decoding method that keeps top-scoring transcription candidates. It is not a direct benefit for a worker with busy hands.
options.better_fit: Use this when choosing the best text hypothesis during recognition.

feedback.intrinsic: The team would focus on an internal recognition step instead of the worker's hands-free need.
feedback.instructional: Decoding helps produce a transcript. Benefits describe what speech enables for users, such as hands-free work.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech can support hands-free operation, helping people work when keyboards and screens are not practical.

payload.prompt: A public service app adds voice commands, but some users prefer typing or need text output. What should the app include?

options.rationale: Speech can improve access, but it should not be the only way to interact. Some users may prefer or require text-based interfaces.

options.error_type: confuses accessibility with speech-only design
options.rationale: Voice commands help some users, but they do not meet the need for typing or text output. Speech-only access can create barriers for people who need another method.
options.better_fit: Use voice commands as one option when users need hands-free input.

feedback.intrinsic: Users who need to type or read output could be blocked from using the app well.
feedback.instructional: Speech should expand access, not replace every other path. Keep text input and output available.

options.error_type: confuses alternatives with audio output only
options.rationale: Spoken alerts provide audible output. They do not give users a way to type or receive information as text.
options.better_fit: Use spoken alerts when users need time-sensitive information without looking at a screen.

feedback.intrinsic: Users who need text output or typed input would still lack the access path they need.
feedback.instructional: Audio output is useful, but accessibility also requires alternatives for input and output.

options.error_type: confuses one accessibility support with full alternatives
options.rationale: Real-time captions can help participants who are deaf or hard of hearing. Captions alone do not cover the need for text-based input and output across the app.
options.better_fit: Use captions to make spoken content readable during meetings or conversations.

feedback.intrinsic: Some users would get captions, but others still could not type commands or receive all output as text.
feedback.instructional: Captions are one support. The broader principle is to provide alternative input and output methods.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Text-based input and output keep the app usable for people who prefer or require text even when speech is available.

payload.prompt: A virtual assistant hears a user say, "set a reminder," then turns those words into text before taking action. Which side of the app is this?

options.rationale: Speech recognition is the listening side of a voice-enabled application. It turns spoken input into written text before the request is handled.

options.error_type: confuses recognition with synthesis
options.rationale: The speaking side is speech synthesis. It turns written text into spoken audio, such as an answer or confirmation.
options.better_fit: Use this when the assistant replies aloud after completing a task.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant's input step would be mislabeled as output, making the voice flow harder to design.
feedback.instructional: Listen for the direction: spoken words become text, so this is recognition.

options.error_type: confuses voice input with screen output
options.rationale: The action is about spoken input becoming text. Screen display is not the key capability in this situation.
options.better_fit: Use this when information is shown visually on a screen.

feedback.intrinsic: The team might focus on display instead of capturing the user's spoken command.
feedback.instructional: This moment starts with the user's voice. That makes it the listening side.

options.error_type: confuses transcription with saving records
options.rationale: Saving records can happen after transcription. The key action here is converting speech into text.
options.better_fit: Use this when the focus is keeping searchable call or meeting records after transcription.

feedback.intrinsic: The reminder command might be treated as a recordkeeping problem instead of a spoken input step.
feedback.instructional: Storage is not the conversion. Speech recognition is the conversion from spoken words to text.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Turning "set a reminder" from speech into text is the listening side: speech recognition.

payload.prompt: A project lead for a smart home app must pick the first feature. Users need to say commands like "turn on the lights," and the app must capture those commands as text. Which choice is best?

options.rationale: Speech recognition captures spoken commands and converts them into text. That matches the first feature: users say commands, and the app captures them as text.

options.error_type: confuses capturing speech with generating speech
options.rationale: Speech synthesis would let the app speak confirmations or updates. It does not capture spoken commands as text.
options.better_fit: Use this when the app needs to confirm actions aloud, such as saying the lights are on.

feedback.intrinsic: Users could hear replies, but their spoken light commands would not be captured as text.
feedback.instructional: Start with the user's need. Spoken command to text requires recognition, not synthesis.

options.error_type: confuses transcription with preparing written text for speech
options.rationale: Text normalization expands written items like numbers, dates, and abbreviations before pronunciation. It does not turn a spoken command into text.
options.better_fit: Use this inside text-to-speech before pronouncing written content.

feedback.intrinsic: The app would prepare written content for speech, while the user's spoken command still would not be captured.
feedback.instructional: Normalization works after written text already exists. Recognition creates the text from speech.

options.error_type: confuses speech input with waveform output
options.rationale: Neural vocoding generates raw audio waveforms for speech synthesis. It is an output step, not an input transcription feature.
options.better_fit: Use this when generating the final spoken audio waveform.

feedback.intrinsic: The first feature would focus on audio output instead of understanding spoken smart home commands.
feedback.instructional: Vocoding helps create speech. Capturing commands as text needs speech recognition.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The first needed feature is speech recognition because the app must turn spoken commands into text.

payload.prompt: A product manager compares two accessibility designs. Design A reads web articles aloud. Design B writes meeting speech into notes. The goal is audible output. Which design fits?

options.text: Design A, because it uses speech synthesis
options.rationale: Reading written articles aloud is speech synthesis, also called text-to-speech. It creates audible output from written content.

options.text: Design B, because it uses speech recognition
options.error_type: confuses audible output with spoken input transcription
options.rationale: Design B converts meeting speech into written notes. That is speech recognition, not audible output.
options.better_fit: Use this when the goal is searchable meeting notes or transcription.

feedback.intrinsic: The design would create notes, but it would not meet the goal of hearing content aloud.
feedback.instructional: Audible output comes from synthesis. Recognition creates text from speech.

options.text: Design B, because it creates written notes
options.error_type: confuses text records with spoken audio output
options.rationale: Written notes are useful records. They are not spoken audio, so they do not match the goal.
options.better_fit: Use this when the goal is accurate meeting records and follow-up notes.

feedback.intrinsic: The product would support reading notes, not listening to articles or other content.
feedback.instructional: Focus on the desired output. If the user should hear it, the capability is synthesis.

options.text: Design A, because it captures audio
options.error_type: confuses generated audio with audio capture
options.rationale: Design A generates audio from web articles. Capturing audio means taking in sound through a microphone, which is not the action described.
options.better_fit: Use audio capture when recording sound before speech recognition.

feedback.intrinsic: The reason would point to the wrong part of the voice process, even though the design choice is right.
feedback.instructional: Design A fits because it produces spoken audio from text, not because it records sound.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Design A fits the audible-output goal because speech synthesis reads written content aloud.

payload.prompt: A team is reviewing a new voice assistant for customer service. Which facts support calling it a speech-enabled solution?

options.text: It accepts voice interaction from users
options.rationale: Voice interaction is central to a speech-enabled solution. A customer service assistant that accepts spoken input fits that description.

options.text: It uses speech recognition, synthesis, or both
options.rationale: Speech-enabled solutions use recognition, synthesis, or both. Recognition handles spoken input, and synthesis handles spoken output.

options.text: It must always replace all text screens
options.error_type: confuses speech enablement with removing text alternatives
options.rationale: Speech features do not require removing text. Users may prefer or require text-based interfaces even when speech is available.
options.better_fit: Use text screens as alternatives alongside speech, especially for users who need or prefer them.

feedback.intrinsic: Some customers could lose an access method they rely on.
feedback.instructional: Speech should add a voice path. It should not force every user away from text.

options.text: It can be a voice assistant or conversational agent
options.rationale: Voice assistants and conversational agents are examples of speech-enabled solutions. They can use speech to create more natural interactions.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. A speech-enabled solution supports voice interaction and may use recognition, synthesis, or both.

payload.prompt: A field service director wants technicians to use an app while repairing equipment. Which expected speech benefits are valid?

options.rationale: Speech can reduce the need for keyboards and screens. That helps technicians interact while their hands are busy repairing equipment.
Speech can increase productivity by supporting multitasking. Technicians can continue work while giving or receiving information by voice.

options.error_type: confuses benefits with audio quality requirements
options.rationale: Background noise still affects speech recognition accuracy. Audio quality requirements must be considered before implementation.
options.better_fit: Use this as a risk to evaluate in noisy field environments, not as a benefit.

feedback.intrinsic: The team might overlook noisy repair areas, causing weaker recognition accuracy during real work.
feedback.instructional: Speech can help productivity, but audio conditions still matter. Noise is an implementation consideration, not a benefit.

options.rationale: Speech can create conversational experiences that feel more human and engaging. This can improve the experience for technicians using the app during work.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech can support hands-free work, multitasking, and more natural interactions for technicians.

payload.prompt: A hospital app lets clinicians dictate patient notes. The design lead must keep the app usable for different users. Which choices support accessibility?

options.text: Provide text-based input as an option
options.rationale: Some users may prefer or require typing instead of speech. Providing text input keeps another access path available.

options.text: Provide text-based output as an option
options.rationale: Some users may need or prefer reading information instead of hearing it. Text output helps keep the app usable beyond speech.

options.text: Assume speech works for every user
options.error_type: confuses accessibility with speech-only access
options.rationale: Speech can improve accessibility, but it should not be the only way to use an app. Some users may prefer or require text-based interfaces.
options.better_fit: Use speech as one access path while keeping text input and output available.

feedback.intrinsic: Some clinicians could be blocked or slowed down if speech is not workable for them.
feedback.instructional: Accessibility means supporting different needs. Speech helps many people, but alternatives are still needed.

options.text: Support users with visual or mobility needs
options.rationale: Speech can serve users with visual impairments or mobility challenges. That is one reason speech capabilities can expand accessibility.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Accessibility improves when speech support is paired with text options and attention to different user needs.

payload.prompt: A phone support bot must hold a two-way voice conversation: callers speak a need, and the bot answers aloud. Which parts are needed?

options.rationale: Recognition converts the caller's spoken need into text. That is required for the listening side of the conversation.
Synthesis converts the bot's written answer into spoken audio. That is required for the speaking side of the conversation.

options.error_type: confuses full voice interaction with recognition cleanup
options.rationale: Post-processing can improve readability with capitalization, punctuation, or number formatting. It is not enough to listen to callers and answer aloud.
options.better_fit: Use this after decoding when a transcript needs cleanup before presentation.

feedback.intrinsic: The bot would not have the full listen-and-reply flow needed for a phone conversation.
feedback.instructional: Post-processing refines text. A two-way voice conversation needs recognition, request handling, and synthesis.

options.text: Processing the request between input and reply
options.rationale: Combined voice scenarios listen to the user, process the request, and respond. The middle step connects spoken input to a useful spoken answer.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. A two-way voice conversation needs listening, request processing, and spoken response.

flashcards.back: Converting spoken words into written text.
Converting written text into spoken audio.
AI apps or agents that support voice interaction.
flashcards.hint: They use recognition, synthesis, or both.

flashcards.back: Some users prefer or require text interfaces.
flashcards.hint: Speech should not be the only option.
